analysis.one_liner: Gives hourly retail, food service, and similar workers a right to request schedule changes and requires advance notice of schedules.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have required employers in retail, food service, hotels, and warehouses to post schedules two weeks ahead and pay extra for last-minute changes, died in House committees without a hearing, markup, or vote; its 39 cosponsors were all Democrats.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would let any employee at a company with 15 or more workers ask for changes to when, where, and how much they work — for reasons like caregiving, a serious health condition, school, or a second job — and require the employer to consider the request and explain any denial, with retaliation banned. For workers in retail, food service, cleaning, hotels, and warehouses, it would go further: employers would have to post schedules at least 14 days in advance, pay extra for late changes, canceled shifts, split shifts, and 'clopening' shifts with less than 11 hours of rest. The bill never got any action in committee and expired when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Hourly workers in retail, food service, cleaning, hotels, and warehouses — jobs where unpredictable scheduling is most common. The bill's own findings note that roughly two-thirds of hourly retail and food service workers get less than two weeks' notice of their schedules, and that workers of color and mothers in low-paid jobs are hit hardest. Workers would gain predictable schedules, extra pay when schedules shift late, protected rest between shifts, and protection from being punished for asking.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hourly retail and food service workers

how_it_helps.text: Employees anywhere with 15+ employee employers could request schedule changes for caregiving, serious health conditions, education or training, or a second job, and the employer must engage in a good-faith process and state the reason for any denial.

Covered sector employers must post work schedules at least 14 days in advance and pay $75 per day for missing that deadline, and must tell workers their minimum expected monthly hours for the coming year.

Employers must pay an extra hour of wages for last-minute added or changed shifts, at least half pay for canceled scheduled hours, an extra hour for split shifts, and 1.5 times pay for shifts starting less than 11 hours after the previous one.

The bill bans retaliation against workers who request changes or complain, and lets workers sue for lost wages plus equal liquidated damages, with the Labor Department also able to investigate and penalize willful repeat violations.

analysis.who_pays: Employers in retail, food service, cleaning, hospitality, and warehousing bear the direct costs: the record-keeping, 14-day scheduling discipline, and extra 'predictability,' split-shift, and rest-pay amounts. Small businesses with 15 or more employees are covered too. Some of these costs would likely be passed on to customers through prices, and employers argue the rules reduce flexibility in industries with genuinely unpredictable demand.
analysis.who_pays_short: Retail, restaurant, hotel, and warehouse employers

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on low-margin businesses — restaurants and small retailers in particular — and would be partly passed to consumers, which the bill text acknowledges by defining employer cost burdens as a legitimate 'bona fide business reason' for denying requests.

The pay penalties for schedule changes could make employers more rigid — less willing to offer extra hours or accommodate swaps — since every last-minute change now costs money, and the exemption lets unionized workplaces waive the bill's protections in a collective bargaining agreement.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — predictable schedules for millions of hourly workers who currently get a week or less of notice — is large and directly addresses problems the bill's findings tie to unstable child care, hunger, and worse mental health. The costs are real but appear modest relative to payroll: they mostly compensate workers for time already committed or disrupted, and the bill's own findings cite an employer pilot (Gap) that saw higher sales after stabilizing schedules. The strongest honest objection is design: blanket pay rules for all schedule changes, rather than just abusive ones, could make employers choppier with extra hours. Overall the benefits to workers likely outweigh the costs, which fall mainly on the employers creating the instability.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four House committees the day it was introduced, none of which ever held a hearing, marked it up, or sent it to the floor, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rosa DeLauro introduced the bill on September 19, 2023, joined by seven original cosponsors, and it was sent the same day to the Education and the Workforce, House Administration, Oversight, and Judiciary Committees.
That referral was the last action ever taken: no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded in any committee for the remainder of the 118th Congress.
The bill gathered 39 cosponsors, all of them House Democrats, and no Republican support ever appeared.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large retail, restaurant, hotel, and warehouse employers, who avoided new advance-notice and scheduling-pay requirements, and the House majority that never had to vote on them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Retail, restaurant, hotel, and warehouse employers

against.what_they_did: The bill sat with the Education and the Workforce, House Administration, Oversight, and Judiciary Committees from its introduction day until the Congress expired, with no recorded action in any of them.

sides.party_line_note: All 39 cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican ever signed on; the bill died in committees controlled by the Republican majority without a recorded vote on it.

industries.note: The bill would require two weeks' notice of schedules, pay for last-minute changes and canceled shifts, and an end to scheduling without protected rest — costs borne by the retailers whose just-in-time scheduling practices the bill targets. Avoiding those costs is why the bill's death benefits them.

Food preparation and serving workers are squarely covered by the advance-notice, predictability-pay, split-shift, and 11-hour rest rules; the industry's interest in stopping the bill ran against its workers' interest in stable schedules.
Hospitality establishments are explicitly covered, including for clopening-shift pay; the bill's death spared the industry these requirements.
Warehouse establishments are explicitly covered, so employers like fulfillment and storage operators would have faced the notice and pay rules; the bill's expiration spared them.
